tagline: A 'flying' fish that never leaves the seabed
summary: Despite its name — volitans means 'flying' — this bottom-dwelling Atlantic fish cannot fly or even glide. It walks over sand on its pelvic fins, probing for crabs and clams, and when disturbed it suddenly fans out enormous, blue-edged pectoral fins like a pair of wings.

stats.size: Commonly about 38 cm; up to about 50 cm
stats.range: Both sides of the Atlantic, incl. the Mediterranean; Canada to Argentina in the west
stats.diet: Bottom-living crustaceans (especially crabs), clams and small fishes

facts.title: It can't fly
facts.text: Despite both its common and scientific names, the flying gurnard cannot fly or glide through the air — which is why some prefer the name 'helmet gurnard'.

facts.title: Wings as a warning?
facts.text: When excited, it spreads its huge, semi-transparent pectoral fins, edged in bright blue. Scientists suggest the sudden flash may startle predators.

facts.title: Walking the seabed
facts.text: Flying gurnards have been seen 'walking' along sandy seafloors on their pelvic fins while they search for food.

facts.title: A drumming fish
facts.text: Flying gurnards make sounds with a special drumming muscle that beats against their two-lobed swim bladder.

facts.title: Digging for dinner
facts.text: It feeds mainly on bottom-living crustaceans — especially crabs — plus clams and small fishes, using a stiff front fin ray to dig into the sediment.
